analysis.one_liner: Requires criminal background checks on all firearms sales at large gun shows.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in the House Judiciary Committee when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every firearms sale or transfer at large gun shows — events with 75 or more guns offered for sale — to go through a criminal background check, closing the 'gun show loophole' that lets private sellers at those events sell to buyers without any check. Event organizers would have to register with the Attorney General, keep vendor lists, and verify vendor identities. Private sellers could complete transfers through licensed dealers or a new class of 'special firearms event licensee' registered to run instant background checks.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary buyers and communities affected by gun violence: people purchasing guns at large shows would know the seller checked the buyer against the national instant background check system, screening out felons, domestic abusers, and others legally barred from buying guns. Licensed dealers would face more competition from non-licensed vendors being brought into compliance rather than operating outside it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun buyers and communities affected by gun violence

how_it_helps.text: It would make it unlawful for any unlicensed person to transfer a firearm to another unlicensed person at a special firearms event unless the transfer goes through a licensed dealer or special firearms event licensee who runs a check through the national instant criminal background check system [S3].

It defines a special firearms event as any event where 75 or more firearms are offered or exhibited for sale, transfer, or exchange, with exemptions for sales from a person's personal collection at their private residence and for members-only hunting club events [S2][S3].

It raises penalties for background-check violations and for serious recordkeeping violations by licensed dealers, and lets states get certified for 24-hour background check processing once 95 percent of their disqualifying records are computerized and searchable [S2][S3].

Event operators would have to notify the Attorney General 30 days before each event, verify each vendor's photo ID, and keep and submit vendor ledgers, creating records law enforcement can use to trace guns used in crimes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private gun sellers and gun show operators: operators would face notification, vendor-ID, and recordkeeping duties; private vendors could no longer sell without routing transfers through a licensed check; instant-check registrants would pay a $200 fee for a 3-year registration ($90 to renew). Gun collectors and hobbyists would face more paperwork when selling at large shows.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun show operators and private firearm sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes real paperwork and costs on lawful sellers: operators must notify the Attorney General a month ahead, verify vendor IDs, and maintain ledgers, and instant-check registrants pay $200 per 3-year license [S3].
It covers only large gun-show events, so private sales outside those events — including between strangers arranged online — would remain outside the background check system [S3].

Opponents of gun-show background check requirements argued such rules burden law-abiding hobbyists and collectors without stopping criminals, who can obtain guns through theft or straw purchases instead; the bill's small, bipartisan-but-tiny support base reflected that dispute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: modest paperwork and fees for gun show operators and private sellers, in exchange for requiring checks on sales that currently happen with none. The carve-outs for private residence sales and hunting-club member events limit how far the requirement reaches, and the coverage gap for non-show private sales remains. But for the specific transactions it targets — large commercial-scale gun shows — it closes a documented gap in the federal check system.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its Crime subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Castle, a Republican from Delaware, introduced the bill on July 28, 2005, joined by Reps. McCarthy, Kirk, and Shays as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill had 6 cosponsors in total — 4 Democrats and 2 Republicans — giving it modest bipartisan support but nowhere near a majority of the House [S4].

The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S5], and on September 19, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security [S5], where it stayed with no further action.
No vote of any kind was ever taken, and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private gun sellers and gun show operators who continued selling at large shows without background checks; the status quo of unregulated private sales at those events was preserved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private sellers; unchecked gun-show sales continued

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred, leaving it at the subcommittee until the Congress expired.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed gun-show background check requirements during this era, pressuring lawmakers not to advance them.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; support was small and genuinely bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with 2 Republican and 4 Democratic cosponsors.

industries.industry: Gun show operators and private firearm sellers
industries.note: The bill would have required them to register events, verify vendor identities, keep ledgers, and route every transfer through a background check, ending their ability to sell to buyers with no check at all. Buyers at large shows would have gained a screen against prohibited purchasers.

Dealers would have gained a new business role processing background checks for private vendors, but also faced increased penalties for serious recordkeeping violations. Some dealers who profited from high-volume show sales would face the same checks as everyone else.

Background checks can screen out some prohibited buyers, slightly reducing the pool of legal purchasers at large shows, but the vast majority of sales would still clear and proceed. The direct effect on manufacturers was modest compared to sellers and operators.
